migrationNotes: Spine: we stand beside a graph with a missing point, walk up to the gap from both sides to see where the outputs head, name that place the limit, then learn to reach it exactly by simplifying, and last see that the value in the gap itself never matters.
Running examples: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for the opening walk and the worked example, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for the learner's own turns, (x² − x)/x for teaching the cancelling idea.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): cal-approaching-a-value-1 (a limit with no gap; its meaning is covered by -10 and the limit screen).

lesson.title: Approaching a value

lead.text: Start on the left of the gap and take small steps towards x = 2. At x = 1.5 the fraction gives 3.5. At x = 1.9 it gives 3.9, and at x = 1.99 it gives 3.99. Each step takes us closer to 2, and each answer rises a little to meet the last.

Now come in from the right. At x = 2.5 the fraction gives 4.5, at x = 2.1 it gives 4.1 and at x = 2.01 it gives 4.01. These answers fall, and they settle at the place the left-hand answers were rising towards.

diagram.alt: A close-up of the graph of the fraction near the gap at x = 2, with a table beside it. Dots on the graph and rows in the table show inputs closing in on 2 and the matching outputs closing in on 4.
diagram.caption: The dots are the inputs in the table. Use the buttons to see the walk from the left, the walk from the right, and both together.

afterFigure.text: Neither walk ever reaches x = 2, and neither is allowed to. Yet the answers from both sides crowd in on 4, as though the graph were heading for a point at height 4 and only that point were missing. The next screen gives this behaviour a name.

lead.text: The number that the outputs crowd in on is called the limit. For our fraction, the limit as x approaches 2 is 4. Here approaching means that x gets as close to 2 as you like without ever being 2.

A graph does not need a gap for this to make sense. Take h(x) = 10 − x and let x creep up on 4. At 4.1 the output is 5.9, at 4.01 it is 5.99 and at 4.001 it is 5.999. The outputs close in on 6, so the limit of h(x) as x approaches 4 is 6. Mathematicians write that in a compact form.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons under the picture to switch between the two graphs, and drag the slider to bring a dot in from each side. Both dots close in on the same height, and the picture reports it as the limit. The gap graph is drawn as x + 2, which is what our fraction equals at every input except 2. A later screen shows why.
A limit belongs to the nearby values. What the graph does at the point itself plays no part in it.

lead.text: Reading a limit from a list of numbers works the same way every time. Here are the outputs of a new function.

reveal.text: You looked at where the outputs were heading and ignored where they started. That is all it takes to read a limit from a list.

lead.text: Here is a second fraction with a gap, this time at x = 3, for the same reason as the first. Try an input just to the right of the gap.

reveal.text: 6.1 is one step on the way in from the right. The next screens find where the whole run of answers ends up.

lead.text: Walking up to a gap shows roughly where a graph is heading, and it needs a calculator. Algebra gives the answer exactly. The plan is to rewrite the fraction in a simpler form that agrees with it everywhere except at the gap.

Take (x² − x) ÷ x, which gives 0 ÷ 0 at x = 0. The top factors as x(x − 1). For any x other than 0 we can divide top and bottom by x, and the fraction becomes x − 1. Near 0 the fraction and x − 1 give the same answers, so the fraction is heading for 0 − 1 = −1.

Dividing by x is allowed because a limit only looks at inputs close to 0, never at 0 itself, so x is never zero when we do it. A result of 0 ÷ 0 is called an indeterminate form. The substitution told you nothing about the limit, so the next job is to simplify and look again.
Many gaps come from a difference of squares, where x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a). For example, x² − 100 = (x − 10)(x + 10).

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2.

workedSteps.text: Putting in x = 2 gives 0 ÷ 0, which settles nothing.
Factor the top as a difference of squares.
Cancel x − 2. Near 2 it is never zero.

steps.headline: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.

workedSteps.text: Cancel x − 3, which is allowed because x is never 3 nearby.

steps.headline: The value in the gap doesn't matter

lead.text: So far every gap has been empty. Suppose someone fills it with a number of their choice. Take f(x) = x + 4 for every x except 1, and declare that f(1) = 0. The graph is the straight line x + 4 with one dot knocked down to height 0 above x = 1.

Walk in from either side and the outputs still crowd in on 5, because every point near x = 1 sits on the line. The odd dot at 0 is never part of the walk, since we never stand on x = 1. The limit is 5 and the assigned value is 0, so the two need not match.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two pictures. Moving the dot changes nothing about where the line is heading. A limit follows the neighbours of a point. The value at the point is a separate fact that may agree with the limit or may not exist at all, and the next lesson looks at when they agree.

lead.text: Here the value at x = 2 has been set by hand, and the graph on either side of it is a straight line.

reveal.text: Moving one point did not move the line around it. A limit follows the neighbours, not the value assigned at the point.

lead.text: Same shape, new numbers: a quotient that gives 0 ÷ 0 at x = 4.

reveal.text: You cancelled the factor that caused the 0 ÷ 0, then let x approach 4. The limit exists even though the quotient is undefined at 4.

lesson.orientation: Separate the value approached near a point from the value assigned at the point.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ask a calculator for (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) at x = 2 and it refuses. The top is 2² − 4, which is 0, and the bottom is 2 − 2, which is also 0. A zero divided by a zero has no answer.
Every other input works without trouble. Put in 3 and you get 5, and 2.5 gives 4.5. Draw all the answers and you have a smooth path with a single missing point, like one plank gone from a bridge.

You can't stand on the missing plank, but you can stand beside it. This lesson walks up to the gap from both sides to see where the graph is heading. It then finds that place exactly, without a calculator, and shows why the value at the gap itself makes no difference.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a limit by cancelling a common factor, and say why the value at the point itself doesn't matter.
intro.whyItMatters: Every derivative is a limit of this shape, where the quotient is undefined at the point.

recap.keyIdea: A limit is where the outputs head as the input closes in. It ignores the value at the point itself, so a 0 ÷ 0 gap is settled by simplifying nearby.

blocks.text: Back at the missing plank, you found where (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) is heading, and you learned to cancel the factor that causes the 0 ÷ 0 so that the answer comes out exactly. You also saw that a value placed in the gap by hand does not move the limit.

recap.nextHook: So far both sides of a gap have headed for the same height. A price list with a step in it is a place where they can disagree, and the next lesson starts at a shop till.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x + 3, what value does f(x) approach as x approaches 2?
hints: Use inputs close to the stated point from both sides.
This line is continuous at the target input.
Insert the target input into x + 3.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Outputs from both sides meet at 5, and that meeting point is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is where the input is heading. The question asks where the output goes.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.
hints: Factor the difference of squares before considering the limit.
Write the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3).
Cancel the common factor for allowed nearby inputs, then approach the excluded input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Factor the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3). Away from 3 the quotient equals x + 3, which approaches 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Factor, cancel x − 3 for nearby x, then let x approach 3: 3 + 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 0/0 is not a value. Factor the top and cancel before letting x approach 3.
Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3) first, then cancel.

questions.prompt: The graph has f(x) = x + 1 for x ≠ 2, but f(2) = 5. Which statement is true?
hints: Follow the neighbouring points, not the isolated assigned value.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The surrounding line approaches 3. Changing one point to 5 does not change the limit.

questions.onCorrect: The limit is 3. The line around x = 2 decides it; the value at 2 does not.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the value assigned at x = 2. The limit follows the neighbouring points instead.
One odd point does not stop the line around it from heading somewhere.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 16)/(x − 4) as x approaches 4.
hints: Retain the excluded input when cancelling the common factor.
Write the numerator as (x − 4)(x + 4).
Approach the excluded input in the remaining linear expression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: For x ≠ 4 the quotient is x + 4, so its limit is 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Cancel the factor that causes the 0/0, then let x approach 4: 4 + 4.

misconceptions.feedback: 0/0 is not a value. Cancel the common factor first.
4 is where x is heading. Put 4 into what is left after cancelling.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 25)/(x − 5) as x approaches 5.
hints: Recognise a difference of squares.
Factor the numerator as (x − 5)(x + 5).
Use the simplified line only for the nearby inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The nearby expression is x + 5, which approaches 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Cancel x − 5, then let x approach 5: 5 + 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting x = 5 straight in gives 0/0. Cancel the common factor first.
5 is where x is heading. Put it into the cancelled expression, x + 5.

questions.prompt: Direct substitution in a quotient gives 0/0. What should happen next?
hints: Both numerator and denominator approaching zero does not determine their ratio.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The form 0/0 is indeterminate. Simplification or another valid method is needed.

questions.onCorrect: 0/0 settles nothing. Look at what the quotient does near the point, for instance by cancelling.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero on top does not make the whole quotient zero when the bottom is zero too.
A number over itself is 1 only when it is not zero. This one is 0/0.

hints: Work out the top first: what is 3.1 × 3.1, less 9?
The top is 0.61. What is the bottom, 3.1 − 3?
Divide 0.61 by 0.1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3.1² = 9.61, so the top is 0.61. The bottom is 0.1. 0.61 ÷ 0.1 = 6.1.
